account: Global Fishing Watch was developed by Oceana, SkyTruth and Google. It processes automatic identification system tracks of tens of thousands of vessels. In Oceana's description, it uses machine learning and cloud computing to identify when they are fishing. Kiribati closed the Phoenix Islands Protected Area to commercial fishing on 1 January 2015. Oceana's Jacqueline Savitz wrote in 2018 that Global Fishing Watch revealed illegal fishing in the area a few months after the closure. The platform launched publicly at the Our Ocean conference on 15 September 2016. The Washington Post reported that before the launch the government of Kiribati had used it to document how a tuna-fishing vessel had operated illegally inside the protected area. That resulted in a US$1 million fine. Oceana board member Ted Danson wrote in Grist that the vessel was the Marshall Islands-flagged Marshalls 203. The fine was against its owner, Central Pacific Fishing Company. A goodwill arrangement to pay a further US$1 million as a grant came with it. The cited sources do not date the fine. In June 2017 Indonesia became the first country to publish its vessel monitoring system data through Global Fishing Watch. Savitz wrote in BBC Future in 2018 that the technology helped Kiribati extract a US$2 million fine, about 1% of gross domestic product. A 2018 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, by economists funded in part by Google, used Global Fishing Watch data. The economists found that fishing in the protected area had more than doubled in the run-up to the closure and fell to nearly zero after it.

Oceana describes the platform's fishing detection as machine learning over AIS data. No cited source says whether the classifier's output, as opposed to the vessel's track, carried the case. Developer (Oceana, SkyTruth, Google) and deployer (Kiribati) are distinct.

fields.account: Global Fishing Watch was developed by Oceana, SkyTruth and Google. It processes automatic identification system tracks of tens of thousands of vessels. In Oceana's description, it uses machine learning and cloud computing to identify when they are fishing. Kiribati closed the Phoenix Islands Protected Area to commercial fishing on 1 January 2015. Oceana's Jacqueline Savitz wrote in 2018 that Global Fishing Watch revealed illegal fishing in the area a few months after the closure. The platform launched publicly at the Our Ocean conference on 15 September 2016. The Washington Post reported that before the launch the government of Kiribati had used it to document how a tuna-fishing vessel had operated illegally inside the protected area. That resulted in a US$1 million fine. Oceana board member Ted Danson wrote in Grist that the vessel was the Marshall Islands-flagged Marshalls 203. The fine was against its owner, Central Pacific Fishing Company. A goodwill arrangement to pay a further US$1 million as a grant came with it. The cited sources do not date the fine. In June 2017 Indonesia became the first country to publish its vessel monitoring system data through Global Fishing Watch. Savitz wrote in BBC Future in 2018 that the technology helped Kiribati extract a US$2 million fine, about 1% of gross domestic product. A 2018 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, by economists funded in part by Google, used Global Fishing Watch data. The economists found that fishing in the protected area had more than doubled in the run-up to the closure and fell to nearly zero after it.
